readings.title: Corrections: preserve the old claim and explain the new decision

required_presentation_changes.prior: A useful notice states the affected claim, the earlier and revised interpretation, the controlling evidence and whether the change alters a material conclusion. It should distinguish the date of the underlying event from the date of correction. Historical editions remain valuable because they show what information supported an earlier reading. This appendix describes the inherited process; it does not claim that a new correction has been adjudicated for any case. The linked correction resources provide the appropriate place to inspect actual decisions and their continuation history.
required_presentation_changes.replacement: A useful notice identifies the affected claim, earlier and revised interpretation, controlling evidence and any material conclusion that changes. The underlying event date remains separate from the correction date. Historical editions show what supported an earlier reading. This appendix explains the inherited process; it is not itself a decision receipt for another case, and its original workflow snapshot is not a current count of corrections. Inspect the linked correction resources, updates and exact-version AI decisions for actual determinations and their continuation history. Preparing or validating those records does not establish that they have been published.

readings.title: Accessible use and translation: preserve meaning across reading formats

reviewed_section_hashes.heading: Plain language must preserve the claim
A low-bandwidth edition needs functional content

required_presentation_changes.prior: French and Spanish editions need to preserve meaning, proper names, source identifiers and evidence states. Technical and institutional terms require particular care because a familiar translation can imply a different legal or administrative concept. The reviewer should compare the translated passage with the canonical English record and its source scope, not merely check fluency. The inherited process requires a translator, a qualified reviewer and a dated approval receipt. Until those decisions occur, a translation remains a draft and should not be presented as a reviewed public edition.
required_presentation_changes.replacement: French and Spanish editions must preserve meaning, proper names, source identifiers, evidence states and institutional scope. Their text should be compared with the exact canonical English version, not assessed for fluency alone. The inherited Phase 202 contracts called for a translator, qualified human reviewer and dated receipt; those contracts remain visible as history. The September 25 user instruction instead authorizes Codex to make explicitly labeled AI translation and editorial decisions without waiting for a human signature. The current locales are fr-CA and es-419. Each accepted translation needs its own input version, terminology findings and dated AI decision. This does not claim independent human review or approval of unassessed translations.

That consistency is the substantive goal of accessible publication, alongside the practical usability of the interface.
